title: Cloud-Native Associates
disclaimer: Independent practice material by Interstitium Labs. Not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by the Cloud Native Computing Foundation or the Linux Foundation. Confers no certificate. All scenarios are original; no exam content is reproduced.

scenarios.title: Two containers, one localhost
scenarios.situation: A developer puts an app container and a logging sidecar in the same Pod. The sidecar is configured to reach the app at http://localhost:8080 and it works — which surprises a teammate who expected containers to be isolated from each other.
scenarios.prompt: Why does localhost work between containers in the same Pod?
choices: Containers in a Pod share the same network namespace, so they share localhost and ports
Kubernetes automatically creates a Service for every multi-container Pod
The sidecar pattern disables network isolation by design
localhost resolves to the node IP, which NATs back to the Pod
scenarios.why: A Pod is the atomic unit: its containers share network (and optionally storage) namespaces. They communicate over localhost but must not bind the same port. This shared context is exactly why the sidecar/adapter/ambassador patterns exist.
scenarios.hint: What is the smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes, and what do its containers share?

scenarios.title: Who manages the ReplicaSet?
scenarios.situation: You create a Deployment with 3 replicas, then notice a ReplicaSet you never created. A teammate deletes the ReplicaSet 'to clean up' and it reappears.
scenarios.prompt: What is the relationship, and why does the ReplicaSet keep coming back?
choices: The Deployment owns and manages the ReplicaSet — deleting it just triggers the Deployment controller to recreate it
ReplicaSets are immutable cluster resources that cannot be deleted
kubectl auto-regenerates any deleted workload as a safety feature
The ReplicaSet belongs to the kube-system namespace and is protected
scenarios.why: Deployments are a higher-level controller: they create and manage ReplicaSets (one per revision, enabling rollbacks), and ReplicaSets maintain the Pod count. Deleting the child while the parent exists just causes reconciliation to recreate it. To remove everything, delete the Deployment.
scenarios.hint: Which object did you actually create, and what does its controller do?

scenarios.title: Exposing the checkout API
scenarios.situation: Your checkout API runs in the cluster. The frontend Pods need to reach it internally, and external customers need HTTPS access from the internet.
scenarios.prompt: Which Service setup matches each need?
choices: ClusterIP for pod-to-pod traffic; LoadBalancer (or Ingress) for external access
NodePort for internal traffic; ClusterIP for external traffic
One LoadBalancer for both — internal traffic should leave the cluster and re-enter
Services can't do both — run a second copy of the API outside the cluster
scenarios.why: ClusterIP exposes the Service only inside the cluster (the default). NodePort opens a port on every node; LoadBalancer provisions a cloud load balancer; Ingress provides HTTP routing. Internal callers use ClusterIP, external users come through LoadBalancer/Ingress.
scenarios.hint: Which Service type is reachable only from inside the cluster?

scenarios.title: Dev keeps breaking staging
scenarios.situation: Dev and staging workloads share the default namespace. A developer's 'kubectl delete pods --all' during testing wiped staging too.
scenarios.prompt: What is the primary mechanism to prevent this, and what does it not do?
choices: Use separate namespaces per environment — they scope names and enable per-namespace RBAC/quotas, but they are not a security boundary by themselves
Use separate clusters — namespaces provide full network isolation automatically
Rename all staging pods with a 'staging-' prefix — naming is the isolation mechanism
Namespaces encrypt traffic between environments
scenarios.why: Namespaces partition names, RBAC, resource quotas, and network policies per environment — 'kubectl -n staging' vs '-n dev' scopes every command. But namespaces alone don't isolate network traffic (that needs NetworkPolicies) or nodes; they're an organizational boundary, not a hard security boundary.
scenarios.hint: What does 'kubectl delete pods --all -n dev' scope that the original command didn't?

scenarios.title: The Service with no endpoints
scenarios.situation: You create a Service targeting app=checkout, but 'kubectl get endpoints' shows none, even though checkout Pods are running.
scenarios.prompt: What is the most likely cause?
choices: The selector doesn't match the Pods' labels — app=checkout vs app=checkout-v2
Services need a ClusterIP assigned manually before endpoints appear
Endpoints only appear after the first request hits the Service
The Pods need a readinessProbe before the Service discovers them
scenarios.why: Services find Pods purely through label selectors — an exact key/value match. Here the Pods are labeled app=checkout-v2, so the selector matches nothing and no Endpoints are created. (Readiness gates whether an endpoint receives traffic, not whether it appears — unready pods show in endpoints with notReadyAddresses.)
scenarios.hint: Compare the selector character-by-character with the Pod labels.

scenarios.title: Create failed on the second run
scenarios.situation: Your CI job runs 'kubectl create -f app.yaml' on every commit. The first deploy works; every later run fails with 'already exists'.
scenarios.prompt: What is the idiomatic fix, and why?
choices: Use 'kubectl apply -f' — it creates or updates declaratively and is idempotent
Delete first, then create — downtime is acceptable in CI
Use 'kubectl create --force' on every run
Rename the resources on each commit to avoid collisions
scenarios.why: create is imperative and one-shot: it fails if the object exists. apply maintains the desired state from the file (tracking last-applied configuration in an annotation) and reconciles differences, making it safe to rerun — the declarative GitOps-friendly pattern.
scenarios.hint: Which command expresses 'make the cluster look like this file' rather than 'make this new thing'?

scenarios.title: Should we split the monolith?
scenarios.situation: A 4-developer startup runs a successful monolith. An advisor says 'microservices are the cloud-native way' and urges a split into 12 services before the next funding round.
scenarios.prompt: What is the sound architectural advice?
choices: Stay with the modular monolith for now — microservices add operational overhead (deployments, networking, observability per service) that pays off only at team/scale boundaries
Split immediately — monoliths can't run on Kubernetes
Split into 12 services but deploy them as one unit to avoid overhead
Microservices are mandatory for any cloud-native architecture
scenarios.why: Microservices trade development-time decoupling for runtime complexity: distributed debugging, versioning, network failure modes, per-service pipelines. For a small team with a working monolith, a well-modularized monolith (with clear internal boundaries) delivers most benefits without the overhead. Split along team/scaling fault lines when they actually appear.
scenarios.hint: What does each new service add to the operations burden?

scenarios.title: Containers vs VMs
scenarios.situation: A manager asks why the team wants containers when 'VMs already isolate workloads'. They worry containers are less secure and just hype.
scenarios.prompt: How do containers actually differ from VMs?
choices: Containers share the host kernel and isolate via namespaces/cgroups — lighter and faster to start; VMs virtualize hardware with a full guest OS per workload
Containers are just small VMs — there is no architectural difference
VMs share the host kernel while containers each have their own
Containers can't be orchestrated — only VMs can
scenarios.why: VMs: hypervisor virtualizes hardware, each VM runs a full guest kernel — strong isolation, heavy. Containers: the host kernel is shared; namespaces isolate (PIDs, network, mounts) and cgroups limit resources — near-instant start, dense packing. They complement each other: containers often run inside VMs for layered isolation.
scenarios.hint: How many kernels are running when 50 containers share one host?

scenarios.title: Can we bet on this project?
scenarios.situation: You're evaluating an observability tool in the CNCF landscape. It's labeled 'Incubating'. A vendor alternative is a CNCF 'Graduated' project.
scenarios.prompt: What do the maturity levels signal for adoption risk?
choices: Graduated means production-ready with diverse maintainers and adoption; Incubating is promising but less proven; Sandbox is early/experimental
The labels are marketing — all CNCF projects are production-ready
Incubating means deprecated — avoid it
Graduated projects are no longer maintained
scenarios.why: CNCF maturity (Sandbox → Incubating → Graduated) reflects adoption, maintainer diversity, security posture, and governance rigor. Graduated (Kubernetes, Prometheus, Envoy) signals safe bets; Incubating deserves evaluation with eyes open; Sandbox is for experimentation. It's a risk signal, not a quality verdict.
scenarios.hint: Which direction does the maturity ladder run?

scenarios.title: The app that only runs on one server
scenarios.situation: A legacy app stores uploads on local disk, reads config from a hardcoded file, and keeps sessions in process memory. It can't scale past one server.
scenarios.prompt: Which twelve-factor principles would you apply first?
choices: Config in the environment, stateless processes (externalize sessions/state), and backing services as attached resources
Rewrite it in Go — language choice is the main factor
Add more servers behind a load balancer — statefulness is fine
Store config in the container image for portability
scenarios.why: Twelve-factor's core: III Config (env vars, not code), VI Processes (stateless, share-nothing; state goes to backing services), IV Backing services (databases, caches treated as attached resources). These three unlock horizontal scaling and disposability — the foundation of cloud-native design.
scenarios.hint: What prevents any copy of the app from handling any request?

scenarios.title: When serverless fits
scenarios.situation: A thumbnail-generation task runs 200 times a day in bursts, each run taking 3 seconds. The team debates FaaS vs a dedicated always-on service.
scenarios.prompt: What makes this a good serverless candidate, and what are the watch-outs?
choices: Spiky, short, stateless work fits FaaS pay-per-invocation — watch for cold starts, execution time limits, and state externalization
FaaS is always cheaper — no watch-outs
Dedicated servers are always better for bursty work
Serverless means no code — this task needs code so it can't use FaaS
scenarios.why: Functions-as-a-Service shines for event-driven, bursty, short-lived, stateless work: you pay per invocation instead of idle servers. Trade-offs: cold-start latency, max execution durations (minutes), no local state (use backing services), and potential vendor lock-in via event integrations. Knative brings the model to Kubernetes.
scenarios.hint: What do you pay for when nothing is running?

scenarios.title: Why everything is YAML
scenarios.situation: A newcomer asks why Kubernetes uses declarative YAML instead of simple 'do this now' API calls for everything.
scenarios.prompt: What does the declarative model buy you?
choices: You declare desired state and controllers continuously reconcile toward it — enabling self-healing, GitOps, and drift correction
YAML is faster to parse than JSON
Declarative APIs don't need authentication
It's just tradition — imperative calls would work identically
scenarios.why: Declarative APIs + level-triggered controllers are the cloud-native pattern: you say what should exist, and control loops drive reality toward it repeatedly. A deleted Pod gets recreated, a drifted config gets corrected. This is what makes self-healing and GitOps (git as the desired-state source) possible — imperative 'do it once' calls can't do that.
scenarios.hint: What happens when reality stops matching the YAML?

scenarios.title: The 4Cs of cloud-native security
scenarios.situation: A breach postmortem lists: compromised cloud credentials, an exposed dashboard, a vulnerable base image, and an SQL injection bug. Leadership asks for a framework to organize the fixes.
scenarios.prompt: How do the 4Cs map these issues?
choices: Cloud (provider config/credentials), Cluster (API/dashboard hardening), Container (image scanning, runtime policy), Code (app vulnerabilities like SQLi) — defend in layers
The 4Cs are four firewall products you must buy
Cloud, Cluster, Container, Code are just synonyms for 'the stack'
Only Code matters — infrastructure security is the provider's job
scenarios.why: The 4Cs model layers cloud-native security from outside in: Cloud (IAM, network, provider hardening), Cluster (API server, etcd, RBAC, admission), Container (image provenance, Pod security, runtime), Code (secure coding, dependencies). Each layer assumes the outer ones can fail — defense in depth, and every finding in the postmortem lands in exactly one layer.
scenarios.hint: Which layer does each finding belong to — the provider, the orchestrator, the image, or the app?

scenarios.title: Whose image is this?
scenarios.situation: CI pulls 'node:20' from a public registry and ships it. After a compromise scare, you realize you can't prove which bytes went into production or who built them.
scenarios.prompt: What supply-chain controls address this?
choices: Pin digests, verify signatures (cosign/Sigstore), generate SBOMs, and gate deploys with admission control — provenance at every step
Pulling official images is proof enough — no controls needed
Rename the image — attackers can't find renamed images
Only use images you built from scratch — public images are banned
scenarios.why: Supply-chain security = provenance + verification: sign images at build (cosign), verify signatures at deploy (admission controllers like Kyverno), pin immutable digests, attach SBOMs (what's inside), and scan for CVEs. 'node:20' today isn't 'node:20' tomorrow — without pinning and verification you're deploying whatever the tag points at.
scenarios.hint: How would you prove a running image is the one your CI built?

scenarios.title: The overpowered deploy key
scenarios.situation: CI uses a cluster-admin ServiceAccount to deploy one app. A compromised pipeline could now own the entire cluster.
scenarios.prompt: What is the least-privilege fix?
choices: A namespaced Role allowing only needed verbs on needed resources, bound to the CI ServiceAccount via RoleBinding — verify with 'kubectl auth can-i'
Keep cluster-admin but rotate the token monthly
Give CI a human user account instead — users are safer
RBAC is optional in private clusters — remove it
scenarios.why: RBAC least privilege: grant the minimal verbs (get/list/create/update/delete) on specific resources in the app's namespace only. 'kubectl auth can-i --list --as=system:serviceaccount:ci:deployer -n app' audits the effective permissions. cluster-admin for CI is the classic blast-radius violation.
scenarios.hint: What is the smallest set of permissions CI actually needs?

scenarios.title: Flat network, loud neighbor
scenarios.situation: By default, every Pod in your cluster can reach every other Pod — including the payments database from a compromised frontend Pod in another namespace.
scenarios.prompt: What changes this default, and what is the recommended starting posture?
choices: NetworkPolicies — start with a default-deny (all ingress/egress) per namespace, then allow only required flows explicitly
Services — they firewall traffic automatically
Namespaces — they isolate networks by default
Nothing — Kubernetes networks are deny-by-default already
scenarios.why: Kubernetes networking is allow-all by default (any Pod can talk to any Pod). NetworkPolicies are the firewall: a default-deny policy (podSelector: {} with policyTypes Ingress,Egress) blocks everything, then you whitelist required flows (frontend→api, api→db). Namespaces don't isolate traffic without policies. Note: policies need a CNI that enforces them.
scenarios.hint: What is the default Pod-to-Pod traffic posture before any policy exists?

scenarios.title: Secrets are just base64
scenarios.situation: A developer says 'we store the DB password in a Secret, so it's encrypted.' You check: anyone with 'kubectl get secret' can decode it instantly.
scenarios.prompt: What is actually true about Kubernetes Secrets?
choices: Secrets are base64-encoded, not encrypted by default — enable encryption at rest for etcd, use RBAC strictly, and consider external secret managers for sensitive data
Secrets are encrypted by default — the developer is right
base64 is encryption — decoding requires the cluster key
Secrets can't be read via kubectl — only Pods can access them
scenarios.why: base64 is encoding, not encryption — 'kubectl get secret x -o jsonpath={.data.password} | base64 -d' reveals it. Real protections: etcd encryption at rest (EncryptionConfiguration), tight RBAC on secrets, separate etcd access, and external managers (Vault, external-secrets) so secrets never live in etcd at all. Never commit Secrets to git unencrypted (use sealed-secrets or ESP).
scenarios.hint: What does base64 decode to — and who can run that decode?

scenarios.title: No more root containers
scenarios.situation: Security mandates: no privileged Pods, no running as root, no host namespaces — cluster-wide, with violations blocked (not just warned).
scenarios.prompt: Which mechanism enforces this natively?
choices: Pod Security Standards via the PodSecurity admission plugin — label namespaces enforce=restricted (block), audit/warn for visibility
PodSecurityPolicy — the current recommended mechanism
RBAC — it controls Pod security fields
ResourceQuotas — they block privileged Pods
scenarios.why: The built-in PodSecurity admission controller enforces the three Pod Security Standards profiles (privileged, baseline, restricted) per namespace via labels: pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted blocks violating Pods; audit/warn modes surface violations without blocking. PodSecurityPolicy was removed in 1.25 — PSS is its replacement.
scenarios.hint: What replaced PodSecurityPolicy in modern Kubernetes?

scenarios.title: Which pillar answers which question?
scenarios.situation: 'Are we erroring more than usual?', 'What exactly did the failing request do?', 'Where did the latency go across services?'
scenarios.prompt: Map each question to metrics, logs, or traces.
choices: Metrics → error-rate trends and alerting; Logs → the request's detailed event narrative; Traces → cross-service latency breakdown
Logs answer all three — the other pillars are optional
Metrics → latency breakdown; Traces → error trends
Only vendor APM tools provide these answers
scenarios.why: The three pillars: metrics (aggregated numbers over time — rates, histograms — for dashboards/alerts), logs (discrete timestamped events with context — for forensics), traces (causally-linked spans across services — for request journeys). Modern stacks correlate them: exemplars link metrics to traces, trace IDs embedded in logs.
scenarios.hint: Which signal aggregates, which narrates, which follows?

scenarios.title: How Prometheus collects
scenarios.situation: A teammate proposes pushing metrics from short-lived batch jobs to Prometheus the same way long-lived services expose them.
scenarios.prompt: What is Prometheus's collection model, and how do batch jobs fit?
choices: Pull-based — Prometheus scrapes /metrics endpoints; short-lived jobs push to a Pushgateway which Prometheus then scrapes
Push-based — every target pushes to Prometheus directly
Prometheus reads application log files
Batch jobs can't be monitored — only long-lived services
scenarios.why: Prometheus scrapes (pulls) HTTP /metrics endpoints on an interval — targets just expose, Prometheus does the work (service discovery finds them). Ephemeral jobs that die before a scrape use the Pushgateway as a buffer. Exporters translate third-party systems (node, databases) into the exposition format. PromQL queries the resulting time series.
scenarios.hint: Who initiates the metrics transfer — the app or Prometheus?

scenarios.title: Dashboard vs alert
scenarios.situation: The team built beautiful Grafana dashboards, but outages are still discovered via customer tweets. Someone says 'we have observability, we just need to look at the dashboards more.'
scenarios.prompt: What is missing?
choices: Alerting on SLOs/burn rates — dashboards don't watch themselves; alerts route to humans via Alertmanager/PagerDuty with runbook links
More dashboards — coverage is the issue
Bigger TV screens in the office for the dashboards
Customers should be given dashboard access
scenarios.why: Dashboards are for investigation; alerts are for detection. You need alert rules evaluated continuously (Prometheus Alertmanager, Grafana Alerting) firing on symptom-based conditions (error budget burn, latency SLO breach) and routing to the right humans with context. 'Watch the dashboard' doesn't scale — machines watch, humans respond.
scenarios.hint: What watches the metrics at 3 AM so humans don't have to?

scenarios.title: Anatomy of a trace
scenarios.situation: A trace shows: one root span (2.1s) with child spans api-auth (300ms), db-query (1.6s), cache-get (50ms). The team argues about where to optimize.
scenarios.prompt: What does the trace tell you, and what is a span?
choices: A span is a timed unit of work with parent-child links; the trace says db-query dominates (1.6s of 2.1s) — optimize there first
Spans are log lines — the trace says nothing about timing
Optimize cache-get — smallest spans are the problem
The root span time is the sum of all logs — ignore it
scenarios.why: A trace = tree of spans, each with name, start/end timestamps, attributes, and parent linkage (via propagated context). Duration math down the tree pinpoints the dominant contributor — here db-query at ~76% of total. This is tracing's superpower over averaged metrics: per-request, causally-linked timing. Tools: Jaeger, Tempo, OpenTelemetry SDKs.
scenarios.hint: Which span consumed most of the 2.1 seconds?

scenarios.title: Logs in Kubernetes
scenarios.situation: A Pod crashed. You need its logs — including from the previous crashed instance — and you want to follow logs across all 4 replicas.
scenarios.prompt: Which commands cover this?
choices: kubectl logs <pod> --previous (crashed instance); kubectl logs -l app=x -f (all replicas, follow); kubectl logs <pod> -c <container> (specific container)
kubectl get logs — the standard verb
Logs disappear on crash — they can't be retrieved
SSH to the node — kubectl can't read container logs
scenarios.why: kubelet stores container stdout/stderr; 'kubectl logs' reads them. --previous gets the last terminated container's logs (CrashLoopBackOff debugging essential). -l streams all matching Pods multiplexed. -c selects a container in multi-container Pods. For history beyond retention, you need cluster-level logging (Fluent Bit → Loki/Elasticsearch).
scenarios.hint: Which flag reaches the logs of the container instance that already died?

scenarios.title: Probes as observability
scenarios.situation: Your app takes 60s to warm up and occasionally deadlocks. You need Kubernetes to (a) not kill it during warmup, (b) restart it on deadlock, (c) stop sending traffic while unhealthy.
scenarios.prompt: Which probes handle each need?
choices: startupProbe (a — gates the others during boot), livenessProbe (b — restarts on failure), readinessProbe (c — removes from Service endpoints)
One livenessProbe handles all three
Probes are only for monitoring — they take no action
readinessProbe restarts containers — use it for (b)
scenarios.why: startupProbe disables liveness/readiness until it succeeds (protects slow boots); livenessProbe restarts the container on failure (deadlock recovery); readinessProbe controls Service membership without restarting (temporary unhealth, dependency outages). Mixing them up causes restart loops (liveness during warmup) or black-holed traffic.
scenarios.hint: Which probe restarts, which gates traffic, which protects boot?

scenarios.title: Is this GitOps?
scenarios.situation: Team A: CI builds, pushes images, then kubectl apply from CI. Team B: CI builds and pushes images, updates a git repo's image tag; an in-cluster agent syncs the repo state to the cluster.
scenarios.prompt: Which is GitOps, and what are its core principles?
choices: Team B — GitOps: declarative desired state in git (single source of truth), pulled and continuously reconciled by an in-cluster agent, with drift correction
Team A — pushing from CI is the GitOps pattern
Both — any git usage counts as GitOps
Neither — GitOps requires Jenkins specifically
scenarios.why: GitOps principles (OpenGitOps): declarative (desired state as code), versioned and immutable (git history), pulled automatically (agent inside the cluster), continuously reconciled (drift corrected). Team A's CI-push model leaves no reconciler — manual kubectl changes drift silently. The pull model also keeps cluster credentials out of CI.
scenarios.hint: Who applies changes to the cluster — CI pushing, or an agent pulling?

scenarios.title: Drift detected
scenarios.situation: Someone kubectl-edited a Deployment's replica count directly. Argo CD shows the app 'OutOfSync'. The team debates whether to fix git or the cluster.
scenarios.prompt: What is the GitOps answer, and what sync policy automates it?
choices: Git is the source of truth — update git if the change was intended, or let automated sync revert the cluster drift; manual edits are the anomaly
The cluster is the source of truth — update git to match the edit
Delete the Argo CD app — it conflicts with kubectl
OutOfSync is informational — ignore it
scenarios.why: In GitOps, git is canonical: cluster drift is either committed to git (if legitimate) or reverted by sync. Argo CD's automated sync policy (with prune for deleted resources and selfHeal for drift) enforces this continuously. Manual kubectl edits become visible anomalies instead of silent configuration — that's the point.
scenarios.hint: If git and the cluster disagree, which one wins in GitOps?

scenarios.title: Safer than all-at-once
scenarios.situation: You want new versions to reach 5% of users first, auto-rollback on error spikes — without manual kubectl during the rollout.
scenarios.prompt: What is this called, and which tools implement it on Kubernetes?
choices: Progressive delivery (canary/blue-green) — Argo Rollouts or Flagger automate stepped rollouts with metric-based promotion/rollback
GitOps forbids gradual rollouts — all-at-once only
Manual scaling — the only safe way
HPA — it does canary analysis
scenarios.why: Progressive delivery automates canary (stepped traffic shift with analysis) and blue-green strategies: Argo Rollouts / Flagger watch metrics (error rate, latency via Prometheus) and promote or auto-rollback. It extends GitOps (desired state in git) with delivery intelligence — the rollout CR describes the strategy, the controller executes it.
scenarios.hint: What automates 'shift 5%, check metrics, proceed or roll back'?

scenarios.title: Secrets in the GitOps repo?
scenarios.situation: GitOps wants everything declarative in git — but committing plaintext Secrets violates policy. The team considers giving up on GitOps for secrets.
scenarios.prompt: What are the established patterns?
choices: Sealed Secrets (encrypted, decryptable only in-cluster), External Secrets Operator (git holds a reference, the operator fetches from Vault/cloud), or SOPS-encrypted files
Commit plaintext Secrets — git is private so it's fine
Keep secrets out of GitOps entirely — manage them by hand
Base64 is encryption — commit the base64
scenarios.why: Three patterns: SealedSecrets (kubeseal encrypts for the cluster's key; safe to commit, decrypted by the controller), External Secrets (commit an ExternalSecret CR referencing Vault/AWS SM; the operator materializes the Secret), SOPS (age/PGP-encrypted files decrypted at sync). All keep plaintext out of git while staying declarative.
scenarios.hint: How can a Secret be in git but only readable inside the cluster?

scenarios.title: Flux or Argo CD?
scenarios.situation: You're choosing a GitOps agent. The team wants a UI for developers and progressive delivery; the platform team prefers a lightweight CLI-driven toolkit.
scenarios.prompt: How do the two ecosystems differ in emphasis?
choices: Argo CD: UI-centric, app-of-apps patterns, Rollouts for progressive delivery; Flux: composable CLI/GitOps Toolkit controllers, lighter footprint — both implement pull-based sync
They're incompatible — you must pick based on your CNI
Flux is for VMs, Argo CD is for Kubernetes
Only one is CNCF — the other is proprietary
scenarios.why: Both are CNCF graduated GitOps agents doing pull-based reconciliation. Argo CD emphasizes the developer experience (web UI, app-of-apps, Rollouts). Flux emphasizes composability (source, kustomize, helm, notification controllers; CLI-driven, GitOps Toolkit). Either satisfies GitOps principles — choose by team workflow, not by hype.
scenarios.hint: Do both pull desired state from git and reconcile, or does only one?

scenarios.title: What the platform team is building
scenarios.situation: Developers wait 3 weeks for environments: tickets to ops for namespaces, DBs, DNS, pipelines. The platform team proposes a 'self-service portal with golden paths'.
scenarios.prompt: What is this called in platform engineering, and how does GitOps fit?
choices: An Internal Developer Platform (IDP) — paved-road self-service; GitOps provides the declarative, auditable mechanism behind the portal's environment provisioning
It's just a wiki — portals don't provision anything
Developers should get cluster-admin instead — faster
GitOps conflicts with self-service — pick one
scenarios.why: IDPs (Backstage-style portals) offer golden paths: templated, compliant, self-service environments. Underneath, GitOps repos + automation provision namespaces, quotas, databases, pipelines from the template — every environment auditable in git. The portal is the UX; GitOps is the engine. PCA covers exactly this platform-thinking layer.
scenarios.hint: What turns 'file a ticket for a namespace' into 'click a button'?

scenarios.title: Why a mesh at all?
scenarios.situation: With 60 microservices, every team reimplements retries, timeouts, TLS, and per-service metrics — inconsistently. Incidents need logs from 8 repos.
scenarios.prompt: What problem does a service mesh solve?
choices: It moves cross-cutting concerns (mTLS, retries, traffic policy, telemetry) out of app code into a uniform infrastructure layer
It replaces Kubernetes — you don't need orchestration with a mesh
It makes services faster — meshes accelerate code
It's just a load balancer with a new name
scenarios.why: A mesh (Istio, Linkerd, Cilium) injects a proxy (usually Envoy) alongside each service: the data plane handles traffic, while the control plane distributes policy. Apps get mTLS, retries/timeouts, traffic splitting, and consistent telemetry without code changes — uniformly enforced instead of per-team reimplementation.
scenarios.hint: What do all 60 services need that isn't business logic?

scenarios.title: Two planes
scenarios.situation: A mesh diagram shows a 'data plane' of Envoy sidecars and a 'control plane' (istiod). A newcomer asks which one handles actual requests.
scenarios.prompt: What does each plane do?
choices: Data plane (sidecars) processes live request traffic; control plane distributes config/policy (routes, certs, telemetry) to the sidecars
Control plane proxies traffic; data plane is just monitoring
They're redundant — either can do the other's job
Data plane is for north-south, control plane for east-west
scenarios.why: Data plane = the proxies in the request path (per-Pod sidecars) enforcing policy at line rate. Control plane = the brains (Istio's istiod, Linkerd's controller) that compute config from your CRs (VirtualService, PeerAuthentication) and push it to proxies, plus CA duties. This split is the mesh's core architecture — and ambient mesh (Cilium/Istio ambient) moves data-plane duties into node agents.
scenarios.hint: Which component is in the request path, and which configures it?

scenarios.title: Identity, not IP addresses
scenarios.situation: In the mesh, service 'web' calls 'payments'. The policy says 'web may call payments' — enforced even as Pods churn IPs constantly.
scenarios.prompt: What identity does the mesh use, and where does it come from?
choices: SPIFFE/SPIRE-style workload identity (e.g., spiffe://cluster.local/ns/default/sa/web) issued as certs by the mesh CA and verified via mTLS
IP addresses — the mesh tracks Pod IP changes
HTTP headers — the app asserts its own identity
DNS names — identity equals the Service DNS
scenarios.why: Meshes issue each workload a cryptographic identity (SPIFFE ID bound to the Kubernetes ServiceAccount) via their CA, delivered to sidecars and rotated automatically. mTLS handshakes verify peer identity — so authorization policies (AuthorizationPolicy, intentions) are written against stable service identities, immune to Pod churn. This is zero-trust networking's foundation.
scenarios.hint: What stays constant about 'web' while its Pod IPs change?

scenarios.title: Canary with the mesh
scenarios.situation: You want 5% of traffic to v2 for 30 minutes, auto-rollback on errors — without changing the app or DNS.
scenarios.prompt: How does the mesh implement this?
choices: Traffic policy (Istio VirtualService weights / Linkerd TrafficSplit): route 95/5 by version labels, with progressive delivery controllers automating analysis and rollback
Meshes can't split traffic — use DNS weighting
Scale v2 to 5% of replicas — traffic follows replica counts
Edit the app to call v2 sometimes
scenarios.why: The mesh's data plane can split by percentage, header, or path: VirtualService rules with weighted destinations (v1: 95, v2: 5). Progressive delivery tools (Argo Rollouts/Flagger with mesh providers) automate the steps and metric analysis. Replica counts don't control traffic share — the proxy's routing table does.
scenarios.hint: What decides which version a given request hits — replica count or routing rules?

scenarios.title: Mesh vs Ingress — overlap?
scenarios.situation: You have an Ingress for external traffic and now a mesh for internal traffic. A teammate asks if the mesh replaces the Ingress.
scenarios.prompt: How do they relate?
choices: They complement: Ingress/gateway handles north-south (external→cluster); the mesh handles east-west (service→service) — meshes also offer ingress gateways unifying both
The mesh replaces Ingress entirely — delete it
Ingress replaces the mesh — you only need one
They're incompatible — pick one
scenarios.why: Ingress (or Gateway API) is the cluster's front door for external traffic; the service mesh manages internal service-to-service traffic. Meshes ship ingress gateways (Istio Gateway/ingress) so one control plane can own both, and Gateway API (GAMMA) is converging the models — but conceptually north-south vs east-west remain distinct concerns.
scenarios.hint: Which direction does each one manage — into the cluster or within it?

scenarios.title: The mesh bill
scenarios.situation: After adopting a sidecar mesh, p99 latency rose 3ms and memory usage climbed 15%. Leadership asks if the mesh is worth it.
scenarios.prompt: How do you evaluate the trade-off honestly?
choices: Weigh uniform mTLS/observability/policy against the sidecar tax (latency, memory, operational complexity) — consider ambient/sidecarless meshes or skipping the mesh if needs are simple
Meshes have no overhead — the measurements are wrong
Always worth it — every cluster needs a mesh
Never worth it — remove it immediately
scenarios.why: Sidecars cost: extra hop latency, per-Pod memory/CPU, and significant operational complexity (debugging through proxies, upgrade coordination). The value (zero-trust mTLS, consistent telemetry, traffic policy) must exceed that tax. Alternatives: ambient mesh (per-node data plane, lower overhead), or no mesh with NetworkPolicies + ingress for simpler needs. It's an architectural trade-off, not a default.
scenarios.hint: What does each sidecar add to every request's path?

concepts: Microservices trade development-time decoupling for runtime complexity: distributed debugging, versioning, network failure modes, per-service pipelines.

lessons.title: GitOps Basics — Core concepts
concepts: Argo CD's automated sync policy (with prune for deleted resources and selfHeal for drift) enforces this continuously. Argo CD emphasizes the developer experience (web UI, app-of-apps, Rollouts).

GitOps principles (OpenGitOps): declarative (desired state as code), versioned and immutable (git history), pulled automatically (agent inside the cluster), continuously reconciled (drift corrected). In GitOps, git is canonical: cluster drift is either committed to git (if legitimate) or reverted by sync.
Principles: either satisfies GitOps principles — choose by team workflow, not by hype.
Drift: team A's CI-push model leaves no reconciler — manual kubectl changes drift silently.

Sync: three patterns: SealedSecrets (kubeseal encrypts for the cluster's key; safe to commit, decrypted by the controller), External Secrets (commit an ExternalSecret CR referencing Vault/AWS SM; the operator materializes the Secret), SOPS (age/PGP-encrypted files decrypted at sync).

Progressive delivery automates canary (stepped traffic shift with analysis) and blue-green strategies: Argo Rollouts / Flagger watch metrics (error rate, latency via Prometheus) and promote or auto-rollback.

concepts: Service mesh: ingress (or Gateway API) is the cluster's front door for external traffic; the service mesh manages internal service-to-service traffic. Control plane: meshes ship ingress gateways (Istio Gateway/ingress) so one control plane can own both, and Gateway API (GAMMA) is converging the models — but conceptually north-south vs east-west remain distinct concerns.

mTLS: meshes issue each workload a cryptographic identity (SPIFFE ID bound to the Kubernetes ServiceAccount) via their CA, delivered to sidecars and rotated automatically. mTLS handshakes verify peer identity — so authorization policies (AuthorizationPolicy, intentions) are written against stable service identities, immune to Pod churn.

lessons.title: Kubernetes & Cloud Native Associate — Core concepts
concepts: The control plane (API server, scheduler, controller manager, etcd) maintains desired state; worker nodes run kubelets that execute it. etcd is the single source of truth — lose it without a snapshot and the cluster forgets everything.
Controllers run reconciliation loops: compare desired vs actual state, act to close the gap. This is why deleting a Deployment pod yields a fresh replacement.
Pods are ephemeral: names and IPs are not stable. Stable identity comes from Services (virtual IP + DNS) or StatefulSets (ordinal names, stable storage).
Namespaces scope RBAC, quotas, and policies for multi-team clusters — an organizational boundary, not VM-grade isolation.
GitOps makes Git the source of truth with an agent converging the cluster. Manual `kubectl edit` against a GitOps-managed cluster is drift and will be reverted.

example.code:
kubectl cluster-info
kubectl get nodes
kubectl get all -n default
kubectl api-resources | head -20
example.walkthrough: Orient yourself in any cluster with these four commands: where the control plane lives, which nodes are healthy, what runs in the namespace, and which resource types the API serves.

pitfalls: Common trap: thinking etcd is a cache — it is the cluster's memory; treat backups as seriously as database backups.
Common trap: hardcoding pod IPs — they change on every reschedule; always use Service DNS names.
Common trap: assuming namespaces isolate network traffic — without NetworkPolicies, all pods can reach all pods.
Common trap: editing GitOps-managed resources by hand and wondering why the change vanished.

sections.heading: Cloud-Native Architecture
items: Microservices trade development-time decoupling for runtime complexity — distributed debugging, versioning, network failure modes, per-service pipelines.
Trade-offs — cold-start latency, max execution durations (minutes), no local state (use backing services), and potential vendor lock-in via event integrations.
Containers — they complement each other: containers often run inside VMs for layered isolation.
VMs — hypervisor virtualizes hardware, each VM runs a full guest kernel — strong isolation, heavy.
CNCF — CNCF maturity (Sandbox → Incubating → Graduated) reflects adoption, maintainer diversity, security posture, and governance rigor.
Common trap — microservices are mandatory for any cloud-native architecture.
Common trap — vMs share the host kernel while containers each have their own.
Common trap — declarative APIs don't need authentication.
Common trap — this task needs code so it can't use FaaS.

sections.heading: Security Concepts
items: 4Cs — the 4Cs model layers cloud-native security from outside in: Cloud (IAM, network, provider hardening), Cluster (API server, etcd, RBAC, admission), Container (image provenance, Pod security, runtime), Code (secure coding, dependencies).
Defense in depth — each layer assumes the outer ones can fail — defense in depth, and every finding in the postmortem lands in exactly one layer.

RBAC — real protections: etcd encryption at rest (EncryptionConfiguration), tight RBAC on secrets, separate etcd access, and external managers (Vault, external-secrets) so secrets never live in etcd at all.
Common trap — it controls Pod security fields.
Common trap — infrastructure security is the provider's job.
Common trap — RBAC is optional in private clusters.
Common trap — cloud, Cluster, Container, Code are just synonyms for 'the stack'.

sections.heading: Observability
items: Three pillars — the three pillars: metrics (aggregated numbers over time — rates, histograms — for dashboards/alerts), logs (discrete timestamped events with context — for forensics), traces (causally-linked spans across services — for request journeys).

Prometheus — you need alert rules evaluated continuously (Prometheus Alertmanager, Grafana Alerting) firing on symptom-based conditions (error budget burn, latency SLO breach) and routing to the right humans with context.
Dashboards — are for investigation; alerts are for detection.
Common trap — kubectl can't read container logs.
Common trap — every target pushes to Prometheus directly.
Common trap — prometheus reads application log files.
Common trap — the root span time is the sum of all logs.

sections.heading: GitOps Basics
items: Argo CD — Argo CD's automated sync policy (with prune for deleted resources and selfHeal for drift) enforces this continuously. Argo CD emphasizes the developer experience (web UI, app-of-apps, Rollouts).

GitOps principles (OpenGitOps) — declarative (desired state as code), versioned and immutable (git history), pulled automatically (agent inside the cluster), continuously reconciled (drift corrected). In GitOps, git is canonical: cluster drift is either committed to git (if legitimate) or…
Principles — either satisfies GitOps principles — choose by team workflow, not by hype.
Drift — team A's CI-push model leaves no reconciler — manual kubectl changes drift silently.

Sync — three patterns: SealedSecrets (kubeseal encrypts for the cluster's key; safe to commit, decrypted by the controller), External Secrets (commit an ExternalSecret CR referencing Vault/AWS SM; the operator materializes the Secret), SOPS (age/PGP-encrypted file…

Progressive — Progressive delivery automates canary (stepped traffic shift with analysis) and blue-green strategies: Argo Rollouts / Flagger watch metrics (error rate, latency via Prometheus) and promote or auto-rollback.
Common trap — keep secrets out of GitOps entirely.
Common trap — flux is for VMs, Argo CD is for Kubernetes.
Common trap — any git usage counts as GitOps.
Common trap — gitOps requires Jenkins specifically.

sections.heading: Service Mesh Intro
items: Service mesh — ingress (or Gateway API) is the cluster's front door for external traffic; the service mesh manages internal service-to-service traffic. A mesh (Istio, Linkerd, Cilium) injects a proxy (usually Envoy) alongside each service: the data plane handles traffic,…
Value proposition — the value (zero-trust mTLS, consistent telemetry, traffic policy) must exceed that tax.

Data plane — alternatives: ambient mesh (per-node data plane, lower overhead), or no mesh with NetworkPolicies + ingress for simpler needs. The mesh's data plane can split by percentage, header, or path: VirtualService rules with weighted destinations (v1: 95, v2: 5).

Control plane — meshes ship ingress gateways (Istio Gateway/ingress) so one control plane can own both, and Gateway API (GAMMA) is converging the models — but conceptually north-south vs east-west remain distinct concerns.
Common trap — control plane proxies traffic; data plane is just monitoring.
Common trap — data plane is for north-south, control plane for east-west.
Common trap — identity equals the Service DNS.
Common trap — the mesh replaces Ingress entirely.

checklist: Get 7–8 hours of sleep the night before — fatigue destroys recall faster than any topic gap.
Bring valid government-issued photo ID and arrive at the test center 30 minutes early.
Eat a real meal beforehand; bring water and a light snack if the center allows them.
Read every question twice before scanning the answer choices.
Flag uncertain questions and move on — return with fresh eyes at the end.
Eliminate the obviously wrong answers first, then compare the survivors.
Budget your time: answer steadily and keep a 10–15 minute review buffer.
Re-run your weakest-domain drill until mastery is at least 80%.
For Kubernetes Basics: restate the 'why' behind each scenario answer in your own words — if you can't explain it, you don't own it.
